parsed.explanation: The worst documented feature is tier-1 state-imposed universal exposure: a division statute confining trans people to birth-sex facilities in all publicly owned buildings — explicitly including airports — with civil and criminal penalties up to $1,000 and bounty suits of at least $1,000 by any private person, taking effect immediately and flagged by a trans legal-risk assessment as 'Do Not Travel'. A recent arrest (handcuffed in a capitol restroom, held in a men's ward) shows enforcement is real. Layered on this, federal entry screening instructs officers to refuse cases with sex discrepancies and to consider lifetime fraud ineligibility, with documented detentions of foreign nationals and multiple allied travel advisories. Counterweights — a state public-accommodations law, a national gender-identity hate-crime statute, pending litigation, unaffected private hotels — are real but do not displace the facility or border exposures.

entry_documents.exposure: Executive order restricts sex markers; February 2025 cable directs officers to refuse cases with document/sex discrepancies and to consider a material-misrepresentation finding supporting lifetime ineligibility; allied governments issued advisories and foreign nationals were detained over visa issues.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid to expiry; the fraud finding is never automatic, requires four elements, and has limited waivers; the passport policy is under litigation.
entry_documents.interaction: The visitor's home-issued passport meets federal adjudication; a marker/appearance mismatch can escalate from questioning to refusal, detention, or birth-sex placement.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Corrections bureau adopted conversion-style policies (hair cutting, hormone removal) for trans inmates and stopped reporting trans prisoner numbers; immigration custody reports forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and sexual abuse of trans men; a trans student arrested under the facility law was held 24 hours in the men's ward.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: National gender-identity hate-crime statute; pending civil-liberties suits challenging the facility and document laws.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Enforcement of the facility statute feeds directly into birth-sex custody placement, converting a bathroom encounter into a custodial exposure.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Division law bars birth-sex-nonconforming facility use in all publicly owned buildings including airports, universities and offices, with civil/criminal penalties and private bounty suits; federal order bars federally funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity; bans exist in numerous divisions.
federal_state_facilities.protection: No such ban in 29 divisions and the capital district; a division public-accommodations law has prohibited gender-identity discrimination since 2020.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Any public building the traveller enters — including an arrival airport — is governed by the division statute enforced by private bounty, which no anti-discrimination law displaces.

care_services.exposure: Not documented for adult visitors; federal orders and proposed reimbursement rules target minors' care and providers, and teachers facilitating social transition face investigation.
care_services.protection: Not documented. No visitor-facing emergency-care exclusion appears in the dossier.
care_services.interaction: Emergency care is undocumented; a guardian travelling with a trans minor faces the sharpest care-related exposure.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: The May 2026 counterterrorism strategy prioritises 'neutralisation' of groups described as radically pro-transgender; a justice-department reward memo invokes 'radical gender ideology'; schools face investigation and prosecution over preferred names.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The strategy states powers will not target mere disagreement; several executive orders have been enjoined.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Raises discovery probability and official suspicion toward visibly trans or advocacy-linked travellers, compounding border and facility encounters.

minors_guardians.exposure: Division bans gender-affirming care under 18; federal orders frame such care as mutilation and direct prosecution of teachers using preferred names; sports bans apply.
minors_guardians.protection: A May 2026 injunction blocked enforcement of the division's minor-care ban; some federal orders enjoined.
minors_guardians.interaction: A guardian with a trans minor faces the facility statute in public buildings and unresolved care access; the injunction is provisional.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: The division hate-crime statute omits gender identity; no division-specific trans violence data is given.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National hate-crime law has covered gender identity since 2009; division public-accommodations protections and functioning courts.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Federal recourse exists, but division-level enhancement is unavailable and under-reporting is likely.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: The challenge to the facility and ID-invalidation law is unresolved; no enforcement data for those provisions, no count of bounty suits or invalidated licences.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Civil-liberties litigation filed within days of enactment; national hate-crime recourse.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Relief is prospective and uncertain; meanwhile the bounty mechanism operates without any agency or prosecutor initiating it.

anchor_checks.comparison: That anchor pairs a universal birth-sex facility and ward rule with routine police stops, fraud threats and extortion. Here the facility and bounty regime is comparable or harsher in reach (airports, private bounty suits) and entry screening carries real document risk, but there is no documented police extortion campaign, so this jurisdiction sits slightly above it.

That anchor has a public-building birth-sex toilet rule with document checks and rejected complaints, but no criminal penalty, no private bounty, no federal entry-document fraud exposure and no documented custodial harm. Those additions place this jurisdiction below 0.35-A.

That anchor rests on a facility rule with removal on complaint and no organised arrests. Here enforcement is criminal, privately monetised, and has produced an arrest with men's-ward detention, plus federal border screening exposure — materially worse than 0.45-A.

That anchor's worst feature is societal hostility with working provincial remedies and prosecutions. Documented operating remedies are far stronger there; this jurisdiction's hostile institutional rules are enforced efficiently, so it sits well below.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime combines a division statute reaching every public building, airports included, enforced by criminal penalty and private bounty, with federal entry processing that treats sex discrepancies as grounds for refusal and possible lifetime ineligibility. Efficient enforcement of these hostile rules is exposure, not recourse. Real counterweights exist — a division public-accommodations law, a national gender-identity hate-crime statute, unaffected private hotels, and live litigation — but none displaces the facility or border exposure, and custodial placement by birth sex is documented. The result is a documented tier-1 universal exposure layered on real border risk, short of the organised police coercion that marks the 0.25 tier.
